assessments.title: Flash Flood and Transport Disruption
instructions: You are acting as the Secretary-level lead for a multi-agency transport and continuity response in a large metropolitan region. Use the facts supplied in the case as authoritative. You are not expected to know a particular city's emergency procedures.
You will make an initial judgement, make the response executable, receive new information, and then respond to a final decision challenge.
Your submitted responses will be locked before later information is revealed.
Bullets are welcome. The word limits are maximums, not targets. Writing style is not assessed.

stages.title: Initial judgement

fields.label: Initial judgement
fields.prompt: What do you think is the central problem, and what would you do first? Explain your reasoning.

information: It is 07:00 after seven hours of intense rainfall. You have been asked to lead the next 6 hours of emergency transport coordination and set direction for the following 72 hours.
Your immediate objective is to protect life and maintain essential movement over the next 6 hours while establishing a credible 72-hour continuity plan.

groups.title: People and essential services
paragraphs: Approximately 140,000 commuters are displaced from their normal routes.
About 11,000 residents in low-lying wards are under evacuation advisory.
Two major public hospitals are operating on backup power. Current fuel is estimated to support approximately eight more hours of backup generation.

groups.title: Transport capacity
paragraphs: 22 metro stations are inaccessible, three bus depots are affected, two intercity rail terminals have restricted access, and 18 major arterial roads are closed or intermittently passable.

There are 600 buses available for emergency redeployment. The rail authority requests 260 buses for stranded passengers. District administrations collectively request 420 buses for evacuation and movement to shelters.
Police can secure only a limited number of priority road corridors at one time.

groups.title: Infrastructure
paragraphs: Drainage pumps are functioning intermittently because of power instability. Structural inspections of some flooded metro assets are incomplete.

groups.title: Information environment
paragraphs: Mobile connectivity is degraded in roughly 40 percent of the affected area.
A false social-media message claiming an upstream dam has failed is spreading quickly. There is currently no evidence of a dam failure.
Different agencies have issued inconsistent public messages about when transport services may reopen.

groups.title: Weather
paragraphs: The weather service estimates a 60 percent chance of another 90 to 130 mm of rain over the next 12 hours.

groups.title: Citizens and coordination
paragraphs: Several of the low-lying wards under evacuation advisory include households with limited access to private transport.

The 600 buses are drawn from both metropolitan and state transport fleets. District administrations manage evacuation and shelters, police control priority-road access, and the rail authority manages the terminals. No single agency controls all resources needed for the response.

fields.label: Make it executable
fields.prompt: How would you use the available transport capacity and coordinate the response across the institutions involved? Explain the principle guiding your choices.

stages.title: New information

fields.label: New information
fields.prompt: Given the new information, what would you change, what would you deliberately retain, and why?

information: Three hours later, the following developments are confirmed:
A structural inspection confirms major water ingress in one central metro tunnel. It will not reopen today.
A substation failure has stopped several drainage pumps. Estimated restoration time is four hours.
The weather forecast improves. There is now a 35 percent chance of 60 to 90 mm of additional rain over the next 12 hours.
The largest shelter district reports that current shelter capacity will be reached in approximately two hours unless additional space is opened.
The rail authority now says it needs only 180 of the 260 buses originally requested because special trains have been added at an unaffected terminal.
Major media outlets are asking the government to announce a single citywide reopening time within the next 30 minutes.

stages.title: Decision challenge

fields.label: Your position
fields.prompt: How does your position change?

options.label: Maintain
Modify
Reverse

fields.label: Decision challenge
fields.prompt: How would you respond to the official's argument? Explain your decision, the most important trade-off or obligation guiding it, and one specific change in conditions that would make you reconsider.

information: At the next coordination review, a senior official argues that the improved rainfall forecast and the addition of special trains mean the government should now redirect most emergency bus capacity toward restoring normal commuter movement. The official also argues for announcing a single citywide reopening target to reassure the public and reduce economic disruption.

assessments.title: LPG Supply Disruption
instructions: You are acting as the Secretary-level lead for a 30-day national continuity response to a temporary LPG supply disruption. Use the case facts as authoritative. Your task is not to recall existing rationing rules or predict the actual market. It is to make and justify a workable continuity strategy under uncertainty.
Your responses will be locked before later developments are revealed.
Bullets are welcome. The word limits are maximums, not targets. Writing style is not assessed.

stages.title: Initial judgement

fields.label: Initial judgement
fields.prompt: What do you see as the central problem, and what would you do over the next 30 days? Explain your reasoning.

information: A shipping disruption is expected to constrain LPG imports for an uncertain period estimated at two to five weeks.

groups.title: Stock and distribution
paragraphs: National usable LPG inventory in the distribution system is equivalent to approximately 18 days of current consumption.
Seven states hold only 9 to 12 days of distributor inventory. Most other states hold more than 20 days.
A centrally controlled buffer, additional to the 18 days above, is equivalent to about five days of national consumption. Releasing and moving it is logistically uneven.

groups.title: Demand
paragraphs: Current LPG use is estimated as 71 percent households, 17 percent commercial users, 5 percent essential services, and 7 percent industrial users.
New household bookings are 22 percent above normal. Duplicate or unusually early bookings are estimated to be 18 percent above normal.
Visible queues have formed in several cities, but there is no national stockout.

groups.title: Supply options
paragraphs: Some commercial and industrial users can switch to alternative fuels, but conversion takes roughly three to seven days and raises operating costs.
Domestic production could increase by about 5 percent within 10 days.
An alternative import cargo equivalent to approximately two days of national consumption could arrive in six to nine days at higher cost.

groups.title: Logistics
paragraphs: Interstate transfers generally take two to five days.

groups.title: Public pressure
paragraphs: Hospitals and large community kitchens are asking for guaranteed allocations.
There is strong pressure to announce immediate uniform national rationing.

groups.title: Citizens and coordination
paragraphs: Some households, particularly in remote areas and lower-income communities, have no safe short-term substitute for LPG. By contrast, some commercial and industrial users can switch fuels within three to seven days, although doing so raises their operating costs.

The central government controls the emergency buffer and coordinates additional supply. States and distributors manage much of the last-mile allocation, while interstate transfers depend on transport capacity and receiving infrastructure.

fields.label: Allocation and execution
fields.prompt: If supply needs to be conserved or redistributed, what principle would guide how the burden and available supply are distributed across states and user groups, and how would you make that approach workable?

stages.title: Day 4 update

fields.label: Day 4 update
fields.prompt: What would you materially change now, what would you deliberately retain, and why?

information: On Day 4, the situation changes:
An unexpected bottling-plant outage reduces national dispatch capacity by approximately 8 percent for five days.
A false viral message claims that household LPG will run out nationwide within 72 hours.
Household bookings rise a further 19 percent within 24 hours.
Two rural districts now report less than five days of distributor stock.
Guaranteed allocations to hospitals and community kitchens are currently being met.
The alternative import cargo is now expected in seven days, with approximately 70 percent confidence.

selectedResponses.label: Evidence check
selectedResponses.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the new information?

options.label: Use the increase in household bookings as the main estimate of the increase in actual household LPG consumption.
Treat the viral message and booking increase as evidence that a nationwide stockout within 72 hours is now likely.
Check actual consumption and location-specific stock before concluding that the booking increase represents a nationwide physical shortage.

feedbackByOption.C: Correct. A rise in bookings shows changed demand behaviour, but it does not by itself establish an equivalent increase in actual consumption or a nationwide physical shortage.
feedbackByOption.A: Not quite. Bookings can rise because households order earlier or duplicate requests during uncertainty. The best-supported conclusion is to check actual consumption and location-specific stock before inferring a nationwide physical shortage.
feedbackByOption.B: Not quite. The viral claim and resulting bookings show public anxiety, not evidence of a nationwide stockout within 72 hours. The case still shows that the most severe stock problem is localized.

stages.title: Allocation challenge

fields.label: Your position
fields.prompt: How does your position change?

options.label: Maintain
Modify
Reverse

fields.label: Allocation challenge
fields.prompt: What would you decide now? Respond to the strongest argument against your position, explain the principle or obligation guiding your decision, state the important trade-off you are accepting, and identify one change in conditions that would make you reconsider.

information: Several higher-stock states object to allocating the central buffer mainly on current days of stock. They argue that some states built larger inventories through earlier conservation measures, that their populations could also become vulnerable if the disruption lasts five weeks, and that repeatedly changing allocation rules will reduce trust in the national response.

They propose a published formula that guarantees every state a baseline allocation and distributes the remainder using factors such as current stock, essential-service demand, population dependent on LPG, and transfer time.

Lower-stock states argue that the buffer exists precisely to prevent the first local shortages and that distributing scarce supply to states with more than 20 days of stock while some districts have fewer than five would delay help until after avoidable harm occurs.

assessments.title: Air Quality Emergency
instructions: In this case, you are not being asked to guess the correct future. You are being asked to make your reasoning visible before you know the outcome.

You will first make two predictions and explain why you expect them. Your predictions will then be locked. You will see a simulated outcome, compare it with your predictions, explain what the evidence may mean, and revise your response.
A prediction that does not match the later evidence can still reflect strong reasoning if it was well supported and you update appropriately when better evidence appears.
Bullets are welcome. Writing style is not assessed.
The word limits are maximums, not targets.

stages.title: Predict

fields.label: Critical assumption or dependency
fields.prompt: What assumption or dependency matters most to whether your predictions hold, and what observation would make you question it?

information: You are chairing a 14-day intergovernmental response group in a fictional metropolitan region experiencing severe air pollution.

groups.title: Air quality and health
paragraphs: AQI has ranged from 430 to 490 for the last 72 hours and is currently 462.
Respiratory emergency-department visits are 31 percent above the recent baseline.
Paediatric respiratory visits are 42 percent above baseline.

groups.title: Source uncertainty
paragraphs: Model A estimates road transport 28 percent, construction and dust 22 percent, industry 16 percent, regional or upwind sources 26 percent, and other sources 8 percent.
Model B estimates regional or upwind contribution at 41 percent, with correspondingly lower local contributions.
Both models have material uncertainty.

groups.title: Construction
paragraphs: Registered large construction sites are estimated to be 76 percent compliant with current controls.
Informal-site compliance is unknown.
Stronger construction restrictions would affect a substantial daily-wage workforce.

groups.title: Mobility
paragraphs: Bus ridership is already 17 percent above normal.
The bus system is close to peak operating capacity.

groups.title: Protection
paragraphs: High-filtration mask stocks available to public facilities are estimated to last approximately nine days at current distribution rates.

groups.title: Regional coordination
paragraphs: Neighbouring jurisdictions have not agreed to binding regional emission reductions.

groups.title: 48-hour response package
paragraphs: Intensify enforcement at registered large construction sites.
Restrict heavy goods vehicles in the central zone during daytime hours.
Add approximately 20 percent bus capacity where vehicles and staff can be redeployed.
Prioritise high-filtration masks for clinics, schools, and high-exposure public workers.
Request neighbouring jurisdictions to reduce major point-source emissions.

note: Citywide air-quality readings can change because of both emissions and atmospheric conditions. Changes in exposure may not immediately appear in health-service data. Source-contribution estimates are uncertain and may change as additional evidence becomes available.
stages.responseInstruction: Make two specific predictions that you think are most important for judging the effects of this 48-hour response. Each prediction should describe one observable pattern. You do not need to predict every possible effect.

groups.title: Observed evidence
paragraphs: Registered-site compliance rises from 76 percent to 91 percent.
Heavy-goods traffic in the central zone falls approximately 14 percent during restriction hours.
Selected roadside monitoring sites inside the restricted zone show modest improvement during restriction hours. The improvement is not consistent across the metropolitan region.
Citywide AQI remains between 455 and 480, with no sustained citywide improvement.
A revised source analysis places regional or upwind contribution at approximately 38 to 46 percent, with moderate confidence. Material uncertainty remains.
Neighbouring jurisdictions have not yet adopted comparable controls.
Atmospheric dispersion remained unfavorable during much of the period. Stronger dispersion may occur during the next 36 to 48 hours, with moderate confidence.
Respiratory emergency-department visits are now 39 percent above the recent baseline.
Bus ridership rises another 9 percent, leaving the system close to operational capacity.
Labour officials report significant income distress among casual workers affected by construction restrictions.

fields.label: Pattern or mismatch
fields.prompt: What is the most important pattern or mismatch between your forecast and the observed evidence? State what the evidence supports and what it does not yet establish.

fields.label: Explanation and alternatives
fields.prompt: What is your leading explanation for that pattern? Give one serious alternative explanation and identify the additional evidence that would best distinguish between them.

fields.label: Revised action
fields.prompt: Based on your explanation, what would you change and what would you retain for the next 72 hours? Explain how your decision follows from the evidence, name the most important trade-off you are accepting, and identify one indicator or threshold that would trigger another material change.

selectedResponses.label: Evidence check 1
selectedResponses.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the 48-hour observations?

options.label: The local controls were ineffective because citywide AQI did not improve during the period
The local controls changed some local indicators, but their effect on citywide AQI cannot yet be isolated
Regional sources explain the citywide result because their estimated contribution increased in the revised analysis

feedbackByOption.B: Correct. The observations show changes in implementation and some local indicators while citywide AQI stayed high. The evidence therefore supports a mixed effect, not a clean estimate of the package's citywide impact.
feedbackByOption.A: Not quite. Citywide AQI stayed high, but several local indicators changed. The evidence therefore does not support concluding that the local controls had no effect.
feedbackByOption.C: Not quite. The revised regional estimate increases the plausibility of a regional contribution but does not establish the cause of the citywide result.

selectedResponses.label: Evidence check 2
selectedResponses.prompt: Which additional evidence would best distinguish whether the controls changed emissions but the citywide signal was obscured, versus whether the controls had little effect on emissions?

options.label: Matched roadside, background, and upwind monitor trends across changing weather conditions
Neighborhood perception surveys collected before and after the response package
Respiratory emergency-department trends separated by age group and neighborhood

feedbackByOption.A: Correct. Comparing roadside, background, and upwind monitoring across changing weather conditions would help separate local emission changes from regional or atmospheric masking.
feedbackByOption.B: Not quite. Perception surveys describe experienced conditions but do not directly distinguish the competing emission mechanisms.
feedbackByOption.C: Not quite. Health-service trends matter for impact but are delayed and nonspecific for distinguishing these competing emission mechanisms.

selectedResponses.label: Evidence check 3
selectedResponses.prompt: Which interpretation of the respiratory emergency-department data is best supported at this point?

options.label: The rise shows the package worsened respiratory harm during the 48-hour period
The rise shows the package produced no meaningful health benefit during the period
The rise is concerning, but it does not isolate the package's health effect over 48 hours

feedbackByOption.C: Correct. The rise is important, but health-service use can lag exposure and other influences remain active. The 48-hour data therefore cannot isolate the package's health effect.
feedbackByOption.A: Not quite. A rise during the intervention does not establish that the intervention caused the rise.
feedbackByOption.B: Not quite. Continued elevated visits do not establish that the package produced no health benefit. The observation window is too short for that inference.

fields.label: Prediction
fields.prompt: What do you expect to observe over the next 48 hours?

fields.label: Why
fields.prompt: Why do you expect this? Explain the causal chain or interaction behind your prediction.

fields.label: Confidence
fields.prompt: How confident are you in this prediction?

options.label: High
Medium
Low

predictions.comparisonPrompt: How does the evidence relate to your original prediction?
predictions.evidencePrompt: Which observation or observations most influenced your classification?

assessments.title: Public Grievance Reform
instructions: This case uses the same reasoning sequence as the previous case, but the system is institutional rather than physical.
You will predict how a reform may affect the service system, commit to those predictions, inspect a simulated outcome, explain what may have produced it, and revise the reform.
You are not expected to know a particular grievance platform or existing government procedure. Use the supplied case facts as authoritative.
Bullets are welcome. The word limits are maximums, not targets. Writing style is not assessed.

stages.title: Predict

fields.label: Critical assumption or dependency
fields.prompt: What assumption or dependency matters most to whether your predictions hold, and what observation would make you question it?

information: You are the Secretary responsible for a 90-day cross-department initiative to reduce a large public-grievance backlog while improving the quality of resolution.

groups.title: Service system
paragraphs: 180,000 open grievances across 12 departments.
24 percent of open grievances are older than 90 days.
Median time to closure is 23 days.
Citizen satisfaction with closed cases is 56 percent.
17 percent of cases are reopened within 30 days of closure.
61 percent of all grievances come from four high-volume departments.
12 percent require action from more than one department.
No additional staffing is approved for the first 90 days.
Departments vary considerably in case complexity and in the proportion of grievances requiring coordination with another department.
Existing dashboard measures are not adjusted for those differences.

groups.title: Proposed reform
paragraphs: Publish a department-level dashboard showing backlog, closure time, and age of open cases.
Set a 15-day closure target.
Automatically escalate unresolved cases after Day 10.
Use dashboard measures in regular senior performance reviews.
Use standard closure categories across departments.
Require senior review of cases open more than 30 days.

stages.responseInstruction: Make two specific predictions that you think are most important for judging whether this reform is working. Each prediction should describe one observable pattern. You do not need to predict every possible effect.

groups.title: Observed evidence
paragraphs: Monthly closures increase 32 percent.
Median closure time falls from 23 to 15 days.
Overall open backlog falls 11 percent.
The 30-day reopen rate rises from 17 percent to 20 percent.
Citizen satisfaction falls from 56 percent to 54 percent.
19 percent of closures use broad categories such as "information provided" or "outside jurisdiction."
Transfers between departments increase 21 percent.
Cross-department cases open more than 30 days increase 13 percent.
The oldest 10 percent of grievances show little improvement.
Recorded closures increase in the final two working days before scheduled performance reviews.
The system records when a closure is formally posted. It does not show when substantive work on the case was completed.
One department introduces a local quality check before closure. Its median closure time is 16 days, its 30-day reopen rate is 14 percent, and citizen satisfaction is 62 percent.
That department also has fewer cross-department grievances than the system average.

fields.label: Pattern or mismatch
fields.prompt: What is the most important pattern or mismatch between what you expected and what occurred? What does the evidence support, and what does it not yet establish?

fields.label: Explanation and alternatives
fields.prompt: What is your leading explanation for that pattern? Give one serious alternative explanation and identify the additional evidence that would best distinguish between them.

fields.label: Revised action
fields.prompt: Based on what you now know, how would you change the reform for the next 60 days, and what would you deliberately retain? Explain how your changes follow from the evidence, state the most important trade-off you are accepting, and identify one indicator or threshold that would trigger another material change.

selectedResponses.label: Evidence check 1
selectedResponses.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the observed pattern?

options.label: The reform improved service quality because cases were closed faster and in greater numbers.
The reform improved throughput, but the results do not show that faster closure consistently produced durable resolution.
The 15-day target caused departments to close or transfer cases mainly to improve their review metrics.

feedbackByOption.B: Correct. Closure volume and speed improved, but reopenings increased and citizen satisfaction declined. The evidence therefore supports improved throughput without establishing improved quality of resolution.
feedbackByOption.A: Not quite. Faster closure and higher volume demonstrate improved throughput, not necessarily better or more durable resolution.
feedbackByOption.C: Not quite. The timing and transfer patterns raise a plausible incentive concern, but they do not establish why staff behaved as they did.

selectedResponses.label: Evidence check 2
selectedResponses.prompt: Which additional evidence would best distinguish deadline-driven premature closure from genuine difficulty resolving complex cases?

options.label: Case-level audits linking complexity, transfer reasons, reopenings, and timing around the 15-day target.
Staff surveys comparing perceived workload, accountability, and confidence in the new review process.
Department trends comparing monthly closure volume, median closure time, and backlog across the 90 days.

feedbackByOption.A: Correct. Case-level evidence can show whether complex cases behave differently and whether weak closures, transfers, or reopenings cluster around the deadline, helping distinguish between the competing explanations.
feedbackByOption.B: Not quite. Staff perceptions provide useful context but cannot by themselves establish what happened to individual cases.
feedbackByOption.C: Not quite. Aggregate trends show what changed but provide limited evidence about why.

selectedResponses.label: Evidence check 3
selectedResponses.prompt: What can reasonably be concluded from the department that added a local quality-review step?

options.label: Its better results show that the added quality-review step caused the improvement in citizen outcomes.
Its better results make quality review worth testing, but the comparison alone does not establish causation.
Its different case mix makes the department unsuitable for learning anything about the quality-review step.

feedbackByOption.B: Correct. The comparison is promising evidence, but differences in case mix mean it cannot establish causation by itself. It supports further testing rather than a definitive conclusion.
feedbackByOption.A: Not quite. The department differs from others in more than the quality-review step, so its stronger outcomes do not by themselves establish causation.
feedbackByOption.C: Not quite. A confounded comparison can still provide useful evidence. It can justify further testing even when it cannot establish causation.
